claim: Microtubule asters play a fundamental role in the spatial coordination of animal cells.
source: Microtubule asters - radial arrays of microtubules organized by centrosomes - play a fundamental role in the spatial coordination of animal cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about aster function.

claim: The standard model of aster growth assumes a fixed number of microtubules originating from the centrosomes.
source: The standard model of aster growth assumes a fixed number of microtubules originating from the centrosomes.
evidence: This is a description of the standard model cited from existing literature.

claim: Aster morphology in the standard model does not scale with cell size.
source: However, aster morphology in this model does not scale with cell size, and we recently found evidence for non-centrosomal microtubule nucleation.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the standard model based on inference from the model's predictions.

claim: There is evidence for non-centrosomal microtubule nucleation.
source: However, aster morphology in this model does not scale with cell size, and we recently found evidence for non-centrosomal microtubule nucleation.
evidence: This refers to previous findings by the authors.

claim: The biophysical model combining autocatalytic nucleation and polymerization dynamics predicts that asters expand as traveling waves.
source: Our model predicts that asters expand as traveling waves and recapitulates all major aspects of aster growth.
evidence: This is a prediction from the theoretical model presented in the manuscript.

claim: With increasing nucleation rate, the model predicts an explosive transition from stationary to growing asters with a discontinuous jump of the aster velocity to a nonzero value.
source: With increasing nucleation rate, the model predicts an explosive transition from stationary to growing asters with a discontinuous jump of the aster velocity to a nonzero value.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the model.

claim: Experiments in frog egg extract confirm the main theoretical predictions.
source: Experiments in frog egg extract confirm the main theoretical predictions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Asters observed in large fish and amphibian eggs are a meshwork of short, unstable microtubules maintained by autocatalytic nucleation.
source: Our results suggest that asters observed in large fish and amphibian eggs are a meshwork of short, unstable microtubules maintained by autocatalytic nucleation and provide a paradigm for the assembly of robust and evolvable polymer networks.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model and experimental results.

claim: Animal cells use asters to spatially organize their cytoplasm.
source: Animal cells use asters, radial arrays of microtubules, to spatially organize their cytoplasm (Wilson, 1896).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wilson, 1896.

claim: Astral microtubules transport organelles.
source: Specifically, astral microtubules transport organelles (Grigoriev et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2013; Waterman-Storer and Salmon, 1998)
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Astral microtubules support cell motility by mediating mechanical and biochemical signals.
source: support cell motility by mediating mechanical and biochemical signals (Etienne-Manneville, 2013)
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Astral microtubules are required for proper positioning of the nucleus, the mitotic spindle, and the cleavage furrow.
source: and are required for proper positioning of the nucleus, the mitotic spindle, and the cleavage furrow (Field et al., 2015; Grill and Hyman, 2005; Neumüller and Knoblich, 2009; Tanimoto et al., 2016; Wilson, 1896).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Individual microtubules undergo dynamic instability.
source: Within asters, individual microtubules undergo dynamic instability (Mitchison and Kirschner, 1984): They either grow (polymerize) or shrink (depolymerize) at their plus ends and stochastically transition between these two states.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mitchison and Kirschner, 1984.

claim: The standard model of aster growth posits that centrosomes nucleate and anchor all microtubules at their minus ends while the plus ends polymerize outward via dynamic instability.
source: The standard model of aster growth posits that centrosomes nucleate and anchor all microtubules at their minus ends while the plus ends polymerize outward via dynamic instability (Brinkley, 1985).
evidence: This is a description of the standard model supported by a citation.

claim: In the standard model, aster growth is completely determined by the dynamics of individual microtubules averaged over the growing and shrinking phases.
source: As a result, aster growth is completely determined by the dynamics of individual microtubules averaged over the growing and shrinking phases.
evidence: This is an inference from the standard model.

claim: In the standard model, the aster either expands at a velocity given by the net growth rate of microtubules or remains stationary if microtubules are unstable and tend to depolymerize.
source: In particular, the aster either expands at a velocity given by the net growth rate of microtubules or remains stationary if microtubules are unstable and tend to depolymerize (Belmont et al., 1990; Dogterom and Leibler, 1993; Verde et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The standard model of aster growth is being increasingly challenged by reports of microtubules with their minus ends located far away from centrosomes.
source: The standard model of aster growth is being increasingly challenged by reports of microtubules with their minus ends located far away from centrosomes (Akhmanova and Steinmetz, 2015; Keating and Borisy, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: Some non-centrosomal microtubules may arise by detachment from centrosomes.
source: Some of these microtubules may arise simply by detachment from centrosomes (Keating et al., 1997; Waterman-Storer et al., 2000)
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Some non-centrosomal microtubules may arise by severing of pre-existing microtubules.
source: or severing of pre-existing microtubules (Roll-Mecak and McNally, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: New microtubules could arise due to a nucleation process independent of centrosomes.
source: However, new microtubules could also arise due to a nucleation process independent of centrosomes (Clausen and Ribbeck, 2007; Efimov et al., 2007; Petry et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Centrosomal nucleation is insufficient to explain the large number of growing plus ends found in asters.
source: Indeed, we recently observed that centrosomal nucleation is insufficient to explain the large number of growing plus ends found in asters (Ishihara et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: The standard model demands a decrease in microtubule density at aster periphery, which is inconsistent with aster morphology in frog and fish embryos.
source: Moreover, the standard model demands a decrease in microtubule density at aster periphery, which is inconsistent with aster morphology in frog and fish embryos (Wühr et al., 2008, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental observations.

claim: An autocatalytic nucleation model was proposed where microtubules or microtubule plus ends stimulate the nucleation of new microtubules at the aster periphery.
source: To resolve these inconsistencies, we proposed an autocatalytic nucleation model, where microtubules or microtubule plus ends stimulate the nucleation of new microtubules at the aster periphery (Ishihara et al., 2014a, 2014b; Wühr et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the authors' previous work.

claim: Autocatalytic nucleation generates new microtubules necessary to maintain a constant density as the aster expands.
source: This mechanism generates new microtubules necessary to maintain a constant density as the aster expands.
evidence: This is an inference from the proposed model.

claim: Autocatalytic nucleation could effectively overcome extinction of individual microtubules and allow rapid growth of large asters made of short, unstable microtubules.
source: We also hypothesized that autocatalytic nucleation could effectively overcome extinction of individual microtubules, and allow rapid growth of large asters made of short, unstable microtubules.
evidence: This is a hypothesis that is tested in the current work.

claim: The quantitative biophysical model predicts that asters can expand even when individual microtubules turn over and disappear by depolymerization.
source: It predicts that asters can indeed expand even when individual microtubules turn over and disappear by depolymerization.
evidence: This is a prediction from the theoretical model.

claim: In the collective growth regime, aster expansion is driven by the increase in the total number of microtubules.
source: In this regime, aster expansion is driven by the increase in the total number of microtubules, and the resulting aster is a network of short interconnected microtubules.
evidence: This is an inference from the model.

claim: The transition from stationary to growing asters depends on the balance between polymerization dynamics and nucleation.
source: The transition from stationary to growing asters depends on the balance between polymerization dynamics and nucleation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the theoretical model.

claim: At the transition from stationary to growing asters, the theory predicts a minimum rate at which asters grow, defined as the gap velocity.
source: At this transition, our theory predicts a minimum rate at which asters grow, which we define as the gap velocity.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction.

claim: The gap velocity arises due to the dynamic instability of microtubule polymerization.
source: This gap velocity arises due to the dynamic instability of microtubule polymerization and excludes a wide class of alternative models.
evidence: This is an inference from the theoretical analysis.

claim: The gap velocity excludes a wide class of alternative models.
source: This gap velocity arises due to the dynamic instability of microtubule polymerization and excludes a wide class of alternative models.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing the model predictions to alternative models.

claim: The mode of aster growth allows the cell to assemble asters with varying polymer densities at consistently large speeds.
source: More importantly, this mode of aster growth allows the cell to assemble asters with varying polymer densities at consistently large speeds.
evidence: This is an inference from the model properties.

claim: Biochemical perturbations in cell-free reconstitution experiments show slowing down and eventual arrest of aster growth with a substantial gap velocity at the transition.
source: Using a cell-free reconstitution approach (Field et al., 2014; Nguyen et al., 2014), we perform biochemical perturbations and observe the slowing down and eventual arrest of aster growth with a substantial gap velocity at the transition.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to methods.

claim: The growth of large interphase asters is an emergent property of short microtubules that constantly turnover and self-amplify.
source: We propose that the growth of large interphase asters is an emergent property of short microtubules that constantly turnover and self-amplify.
evidence: This is a conclusion from combining theory and experiments.

claim: The polymerization rate vg for large asters growing in Xenopus egg cytoplasm is 30 μm/min.
source: Polymerization rate	vg	30 μm/min	Measured from growing plus ends and EB1 comets
evidence: This is measured from experimental data.

claim: The depolymerization rate vs for large asters growing in Xenopus egg cytoplasm is 42 μm/min.
source: Depolymerization rate	vs	42 μm/min	Measured from shrinking plus ends (Ishihara et al., 2014a)
evidence: This is measured from experimental data with a citation.

claim: The catastrophe rate fcat for large asters growing in Xenopus egg cytoplasm is 3.3 min−1.
source: Catastrophe rate	fc⁢a⁢t	3.3 min−1	Measured from EB1 comet lifetimes (see Materials and methods)
evidence: This is measured from experimental data.

claim: The rescue rate fres for large asters growing in Xenopus egg cytoplasm is 2.0±0.3 min−1.
source: Rescue rate	fr⁢e⁢s	2.0±0.3 min−1	Estimated from Equations (4) and (6)
evidence: This is estimated from theoretical equations.

claim: The autocatalytic nucleation rate r for large asters growing in Xenopus egg cytoplasm is 2.1±0.2 min−1.
source: Autocatalytic nucleation rate	r	2.1±0.2 min−1	Estimated from Equations (4) and (6)
evidence: This is estimated from theoretical equations.

claim: The carrying capacity of growing ends K for large asters growing in Xenopus egg cytoplasm is 0.4 μm−2.
source: Carrying capacity of growing ends	K	0.4 μm−2	Estimated from comparing Cgb⁢u⁢l⁢k to predicted (see SI)
evidence: This is estimated from comparing data to model predictions.

claim: The mean microtubule length for large asters growing in Xenopus egg cytoplasm is 16 ± 2 μm.
source: Mean microtubule length	⟨l⟩	16 ± 2 μm	Estimated from from dynamics parameters (see SI)
evidence: This is estimated from dynamics parameters.

claim: The aster velocity V for large asters growing in Xenopus egg cytoplasm is 22.3±2.6 μm/min.
source: Aster velocity	V	22.3±2.6 μm/min	Measured from rate of aster radius increase
evidence: This is measured from experimental data.

claim: The gap velocity Vgap for large asters growing in Xenopus egg cytoplasm is 12.8±1.7 μm/min.
source: Gap velocity	Vg⁢a⁢p	12.8±1.7 μm/min	Measured from aster growth at 320 nM MCAK-Q710
evidence: This is measured from experimental data.

claim: The bulk growing plus end density Cgbulk for large asters growing in Xenopus egg cytoplasm is 0.053±0.030 μm−2.
source: Bulk growing plus end density	Cgb⁢u⁢l⁢k	0.053±0.030 μm−2	Measured from EB1 comet density (Ishihara et al., 2014a)
evidence: This is measured from experimental data with a citation.

claim: Parameter J describes the tendency of microtubules to grow or shrink.
source: This parameter describes the tendency of microtubules to grow or shrink.
evidence: This is a definition of the parameter J.

claim: In the standard model with bounded dynamics, microtubule loss is balanced by nucleation of new microtubules at the centrosomes.
source: This microtubule loss is balanced by nucleation of new microtubules at the centrosomes, the only place where nucleation is allowed in the standard model.
evidence: This is a description of the standard model.

claim: In the collective growth regime, growth occurs because more microtubules are nucleated than lost, and new microtubules are typically nucleated further along the expansion direction.
source: The growth occurs because more microtubules are nucleated than lost, and new microtubules are typically nucleated further along the expansion direction.
evidence: This is an explanation of the mechanism in the new model.

claim: Self-amplifying propagation of microtubules is possible only for sufficiently high nucleation rates necessary to overcome microtubule loss and sustain collective growth.
source: As we show below, this self-amplifying propagation of microtubules is possible only for sufficiently high nucleation rates necessary to overcome microtubule loss and sustain collective growth.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model that is demonstrated later.

claim: The nucleation rate could depend on the local density of growing plus ends if they serve as nucleation sites or the local polymer density if nucleation occurs throughout a microtubule.
source: This rate could depend on the local density of growing plus ends if they serve as nucleation sites or the local polymer density if nucleation occurs throughout a microtubule.
evidence: This describes possible mechanisms for nucleation in the model.

claim: New microtubules have zero length and tend to grow radially due to mechanical interactions with the existing microtubule network.
source: The new microtubules have zero length and tend to grow radially due to mechanical interactions with the existing microtubule network.
evidence: This is an assumption of the model.

claim: Non-centrosomal microtubules disappear when they shrink back to their minus ends.
source: These non-centrosomal microtubules disappear when they shrink back to their minus ends.
evidence: This is an assumption of the model.

claim: The model assumptions are broadly consistent with known microtubule physiology.
source: Our assumptions are broadly consistent with known microtubule physiology (Clausen and Ribbeck, 2007; Petry et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: There is strong evidence for nucleation away from centrosomes in egg extract by microtubule counting in growing asters.
source: and we found strong evidence for nucleation away from centrosomes in egg extract by microtubule counting in growing asters (Ishihara et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Without negative feedback, autocatalytic processes lead to exponential growth.
source: Without negative feedback, autocatalytic processes lead to exponential growth, but there are several lines of evidence for an apparent 'carrying capacity' of microtubules in a given cytoplasmic volume (Clausen and Ribbeck, 2007; Ishihara et al., 2014a; Petry et al., 2013).
evidence: This is general knowledge about autocatalytic processes, with citations supporting the existence of carrying capacity.

claim: There is evidence for an apparent 'carrying capacity' of microtubules in a given cytoplasmic volume.
source: Without negative feedback, autocatalytic processes lead to exponential growth, but there are several lines of evidence for an apparent 'carrying capacity' of microtubules in a given cytoplasmic volume (Clausen and Ribbeck, 2007; Ishihara et al., 2014a; Petry et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Saturation is inevitable since the building blocks of microtubules are present at a fixed concentration.
source: Saturation is inevitable since the building blocks of microtubules are present at a fixed concentration.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on biological constraints.

claim: Autocatalytic nucleation is expressed as a logistic function of the local density of growing plus ends, which is qualitatively consistent with local depletion of nucleation factors such as the gamma-tubulin ring complex.
source: In our model, we impose a carrying capacity by expressing autocatalytic nucleation as a logistic function of the local density of growing plus ends, which is qualitatively consistent with local depletion of nucleation factors such as the gamma-tubulin ring complex.
evidence: This is a modeling choice consistent with biological mechanisms.

claim: The type of negative feedback does not affect the rate of aster growth, which is determined entirely by the dynamics at the leading edge of a growing aster where the microtubule density is small and negative feedback can be neglected.
source: In SI, we show that the type of negative feedback does not affect the rate of aster growth, which is determined entirely by the dynamics at the leading edge of a growing aster where the microtubule density is small and negative feedback can be neglected.
evidence: This is a result from the theoretical analysis in the SI.

claim: With relatively low nucleation rates and J<0, microtubule populations reached a steady-state profile confined near the centrosome reminiscent of an aster in the standard model with bounded microtubule dynamics.
source: With relatively low nucleation rates and J<0, microtubule populations reached a steady-state profile confined near the centrosome reminiscent of an aster in the standard model with bounded microtubule dynamics (Figure 2A left).
evidence: This is a result from numerical simulations shown in Figure 2A.

claim: When the nucleation rate was increased, the microtubule populations expanded as a traveling wave with an approximately invariant shape and constant microtubule density at the periphery.
source: When the nucleation rate was increased, the microtubule populations expanded as a traveling wave with an approximately invariant shape and constant microtubule density at the periphery (Figure 2A right)
evidence: This is a result from numerical simulations shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The traveling wave behavior is consistent with the growth of interphase asters in reconstitution experiments.
source: consistent with the growth of interphase asters in our reconstitution experiments (Figure 2B and Ishihara et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and a citation.

claim: The model predicted two qualitatively different states: stationary and growing asters.
source: Thus, our model predicted two qualitatively different states: stationary and growing asters.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the numerical simulations.

claim: Asters expand at a constant rate with time-invariant profiles of the plus end density.
source: Experimental measurements confirm that asters expand at a constant rate with time-invariant profiles of the plus end density, as predicted by our model.
evidence: This is confirmed by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The plus end densities were estimated as EB1 comet density during aster growth.
source: The plus end densities were estimated as EB1 comet density during aster growth as previously described (Ishihara et al., 2014a).
evidence: This describes the experimental method with a citation.

claim: In the absence of autocatalytic nucleation (r=0), the model reduces to the standard model and predicts that asters only grow when J>0 with V=J.
source: In the absence of autocatalytic nucleation (r=0), our model reduces to the standard model and predicts that asters only grow when J>0 with V=J (Figure 3A blue line).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and is a result from the analytical solution.

claim: When nucleation is allowed (r>0), the aster velocity increases with r and asters can grow even when individual microtubules are unstable J<0.
source: When nucleation is allowed (r>0), the aster velocity increases with r and asters can grow even when individual microtubules are unstable J<0 (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and B and is a result from the analytical solution.

claim: During collective growth, the aster expands radially because more microtubules are nucleated than lost at the front.
source: During this collective growth, the aster expands radially because more microtubules are nucleated than lost at the front.
evidence: This is an explanation of the mechanism from the model.

claim: In the aster bulk, nucleation is reduced from the carrying capacity, and the aster exists in the dynamic balance between microtubule gain due to nucleation and loss due to depolymerization.
source: In the aster bulk, nucleation is reduced from the carrying capacity, and the aster exists in the dynamic balance between microtubule gain due to nucleation and loss due to depolymerization.
evidence: This is an explanation of the mechanism from the model.

claim: Since microtubules are in the bounded regime, their lifetime is short, and they disappear before reaching an appreciable length.
source: Since microtubules are in the bounded regime, their lifetime is short, and they disappear before reaching an appreciable length.
evidence: This is an inference from the bounded regime definition.

claim: Nucleation not only increases the number of microtubules, but also controls the growth rate and spatial organization of asters enabling them to span length scales far exceeding the length of an individual microtubule.
source: Thus, nucleation not only increases the number of microtubules, but also controls the growth rate and spatial organization of asters enabling them to span length scales far exceeding the length of an individual microtubule.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model analysis.

claim: Microtubules constantly disappear as their length shrinks to zero, and the nucleation of new microtubules needs to occur frequently enough to overcome the microtubule loss.
source: Indeed, microtubules constantly disappear as their length shrinks to zero, and the nucleation of new microtubules needs to occur frequently enough to overcome the microtubule loss.
evidence: This is an explanation of the critical nucleation rate.

claim: The right hand side of the critical nucleation rate equation is the inverse of the average time that a microtubule spends in the growing state before shrinking to zero-length and disappearing.
source: The right hand side of this equation is the inverse of the average time that a microtubule spends in the growing state before shrinking to zero-length and disappearing (SI).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the critical nucleation rate equation.

claim: Aster growth requires, on average, a microtubule to nucleate at least one new microtubule during its lifetime.
source: Thus, aster growth requires, on average, a microtubule to nucleate at least one new microtubule during its lifetime.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the critical nucleation rate condition.

claim: The critical nucleation rate conveys the main implication of the theory: the balance between polymerization dynamics and autocatalytic nucleation defines the quantitative condition for continuous aster growth.
source: The critical nucleation rate conveys the main implication of our theory: the balance between polymerization dynamics and autocatalytic nucleation defines the quantitative condition for continuous aster growth.
evidence: This is a summary of the theoretical findings.

claim: The finite jump in the aster velocity is a consequence of microtubules with finite length undergoing dynamic instability.
source: This finite jump in the aster velocity is a consequence of microtubules with finite length undergoing dynamic instability
evidence: This is an explanation of the gap velocity.

claim: The finite jump in aster velocity is in sharp contrast to the behavior of reaction-diffusion systems, where traveling fronts typically become infinitesimally slow before ceasing to propagate.
source: and is in sharp contrast to the behavior of reaction-diffusion systems, where traveling fronts typically become infinitesimally slow before ceasing to propagate (Chang and Ferrell, 2013; Hallatschek and Korolev, 2009; Méndez et al., 2007; van Saarloos, 2003).
evidence: This is a comparison to other models with citations.

claim: The shorter the microtubules, the more explosive the transition becomes.
source: Thus, the shorter the microtubules, the more explosive this transition becomes.
evidence: This is an inference from the relationship between Vgap and microtubule length.

claim: The density is close to zero during the transition from stationary to growing asters, but quickly increases as the nucleation rate becomes larger.
source: Thus, the density is close to zero during the transition from stationary to growing asters, but quickly increases as the nucleation rate becomes larger.
evidence: This is an inference from the relationship between density and r-rc.

claim: Cells can achieve rapid aster growth while keeping the density of the resulting microtubule network sufficiently low.
source: As a result, cells can achieve rapid aster growth while keeping the density of the resulting microtubule network sufficiently low.
evidence: This is an inference from the model properties.

claim: The low density might be beneficial because of its mechanical properties or because it simply requires less tubulin to produce and energy to maintain.
source: The low density might be beneficial because of its mechanical properties or because it simply requires less tubulin to produce and energy to maintain.
evidence: This is speculation about the biological significance.

claim: In all cases of parameter tuning, the onset of aster growth is accompanied by a discontinuous increase in the aster velocity.
source: In all cases, we find that the onset of aster growth is accompanied by a discontinuous increase in the aster velocity.
evidence: This is a general result from the theoretical analysis.

claim: The finite jump in aster velocity is predicted in a wide range of alternative scenarios including feedback regulation of plus end dynamics and aster growth by microtubule polymer-stimulated nucleation.
source: The finite jump in aster velocity is similarly predicted in a wide range of alternative scenarios including (i) feedback regulation of plus end dynamics (SI and Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and (ii) aster growth by microtubule polymer-stimulated nucleation (SI and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in supplementary figures and is a result from additional theoretical analysis.

claim: The gap velocity is a general prediction of the collective behavior of microtubules that are short-lived.
source: In summary, the gap velocity is a general prediction of the collective behavior of microtubules that are short-lived.
evidence: This is a summary of the theoretical findings.

claim: It is possible to transform a growing interphase aster to a small, stationary aster by tuning polymerization dynamics and/or nucleation via biochemical perturbations in Xenopus egg extract.
source: Based on our theory, we reasoned that it would be possible to transform a growing interphase aster to a small, stationary aster by tuning polymerization dynamics and/or nucleation via biochemical perturbations in Xenopus egg extract.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the theory that is tested experimentally.

claim: Reconstitution experiments were performed in undiluted interphase cytoplasm supplied with anti-Aurora kinase A antibody coated beads, which nucleate microtubules and initiate aster growth under the coverslip.
source: To this end, we performed reconstitution experiments in undiluted interphase cytoplasm supplied with anti-Aurora kinase A antibody coated beads, which nucleate microtubules and initiate aster growth under the coverslip (Field et al., 2014; Ishihara et al., 2014a).
evidence: This describes the experimental method with citations.

claim: MCAK/KIF2C is classically characterized as the main catastrophe-promoting factor in the extract system.
source: We settled on perturbation of MCAK/KIF2C, classically characterized as the main catastrophe-promoting factor in the extract system (Kinoshita et al., 2001; Walczak et al., 1996)
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: In control reactions, aster radius increased at velocities of 20.3±3.1 μm/min (n = 21 asters).
source: In control reactions, aster radius, visualized by the plus end marker EB1-mApple, increased at velocities of 20.3±3.1 μm/min (n = 21 asters).
evidence: This is measured from experimental data.

claim: No detectable changes to aster growth were observed with the addition of the wild type MCAK protein.
source: We saw no detectable changes to aster growth with the addition of the wild type MCAK protein.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: Addition of MCAK-Q710 decreased aster velocity.
source: In contrast, addition of MCAK-Q710 (Moore and Wordeman, 2004) decreased aster velocity (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and B and is an experimental observation.

claim: At concentrations of MCAK-Q710 above 320 nM, most asters had small radii with very few microtubules growing from the Aurora A beads.
source: At concentrations of MCAK-Q710 above 320 nM, most asters had small radii with very few microtubules growing from the Aurora A beads.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: The behavior at high MCAK-Q710 concentrations is consistent with any change of parameter(s) that reduces the aster velocity and arrests growth.
source: In our model, this behavior is consistent with any change of parameter(s) that reduces the aster velocity (Equation 4) and arrests growth.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results in the context of the model.

claim: At 320 nM MCAK-Q710 concentration, bimodal behavior was observed with some asters increasing in radius at moderate rates while other asters maintained a stable size before disappearing.
source: At 320 nM MCAK-Q710 concentration, we observed bimodal behavior. Some asters increased in radius at moderate rates, while other asters maintained a stable size before disappearing, presumably due to the decrease of centrosomal nucleation over time (Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Ishihara et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in supplementary figures.

claim: No asters were observed growing at velocities between 0 and 9 μm/min at 320 nM MCAK-Q710.
source: In particular, we observed no asters growing at velocities between 0 and 9 μm/min (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 4B and supplementary figures.

claim: Experiments with Tetrahymena pellicles as initiating centers confirmed that the failure of aster growth at high concentrations of MCAK-Q710 is caused by changes in aster growth rather than nucleation from the beads.
source: To confirm that the failure of aster growth at high concentrations of MCAK-Q710 is caused by the changes in aster growth rather than nucleation from the beads, we repeated the experiments with Tetrahymena pellicles as the initiating centers instead of Aurora A beads.
evidence: This is an experimental control.

claim: Pellicle initiated asters exhibited a similar critical concentration of MCAK-Q710 compared to Aurora A bead asters.
source: We found pellicle initiated asters to exhibit a similar critical concentration of MCAK-Q710 compared to Aurora A bead asters.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: A significant number of microtubules persisted on pellicles even after 60 min at the highest concentration of MCAK-Q710, while the majority of Aurora A beads lost growing microtubules over time.
source: While the majority of Aurora A beads subjected to the highest concentration of MCAK-Q710 lost growing microtubules over time, a significant number of microtubules persisted on pellicles even after 60 min (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The radii of pellicle asters at high MCAK-Q710 concentrations did not change, consistent with the prediction of stationary asters.
source: The radii of these asters did not change, consistent with our prediction of stationary asters.
evidence: This is an experimental observation consistent with the model prediction.

claim: The pellicle experiments confirmed the main experimental result of small, stationary asters and that the nature of transition is consistent with the existence of a gap velocity.
source: Thus, the pellicle experiments confirmed our main experimental result of small, stationary asters and that the nature of transition is consistent with the existence of a gap velocity.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Neither the polymerization nor the catastrophe rate changed at the MCAK-Q710 concentrations corresponding to the transition between growing and stationary asters.
source: Neither the polymerization nor the catastrophe rate changed at the MCAK-Q710 concentrations corresponding to the transition between growing and stationary asters (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in supplementary figures.

claim: MCAK-Q710 has been reported to reduce microtubule polymer levels in cells.
source: MCAK-Q710 has been reported to reduce microtubule polymer levels in cells (Moore and Wordeman, 2004)
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The precise effect of MCAK-Q710 on polymerization dynamics and/or nucleation remains unknown.
source: but its precise effect on polymerization dynamics and/or nucleation remains unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: The experimental data are consistent with three scenarios for how MCAK-Q710 antagonizes microtubule assembly: increased depolymerization rate, decreased rescue rate, and/or decreased nucleation rate.
source: Our data are consistent with the following three scenarios for how MCAK-Q710 antagonizes microtubule assembly: (i) increased depolymerization rate, (ii) decreased rescue rate, and/or (iii) decreased nucleation rate.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: The standard model of aster growth may not explain the morphology of asters observed in all animal cells, including those of extreme size.
source: It has not been clear whether the standard model of aster growth can explain the morphology of asters observed in all animal cells, including those of extreme size (Mitchison et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about uncertainty in the field with a citation.

claim: A biophysical framework incorporating microtubule polymerization dynamics and autocatalytic nucleation was constructed.
source: To resolve this question, we constructed a biophysical framework that incorporates microtubule polymerization dynamics and autocatalytic nucleation.
evidence: This describes the work done in the manuscript.

claim: Numerical simulations and analytical solutions recapitulated both stationary and continuously growing asters in a parameter-dependent manner.
source: Numerical simulations and analytical solutions (Figures 2 and 3, and Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2) recapitulated both stationary and continuously growing asters in a parameter-dependent manner.
evidence: This is shown in the figures and is a result from the theoretical work.

claim: The explosive transition from 'growth' to 'no growth' was predicted to involve a finite aster velocity, which was confirmed in biochemical experiments.
source: Interestingly, the explosive transition from 'growth' to 'no growth' was predicted to involve a finite aster velocity, which we confirmed in biochemical experiments (Figure 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 and combines theoretical predictions with experimental data.

claim: The biophysical model offers a biologically appealing explanation to aster growth and allows estimation of parameters that are not directly accessible: the rescue and autocatalytic nucleation rates.
source: Our biophysical model offers a biologically appealing explanation to aster growth and allows us to estimate parameters that are not directly accessible: the rescue and autocatalytic nucleation rates.
evidence: This is a summary of the model's utility.

claim: The inferred value of autocatalytic nucleation r = 2.1 min−1 is comparable to previous estimates: 1.5 min−1 and 1 min−1 in meiotic egg extract supplemented with RanGTP.
source: Our inferred value of autocatalytic nucleation r = 2.1 min−1 is comparable to previous estimates: 1.5 min−1(Clausen and Ribbeck, 2007) and 1 min−1 (Petry et al., 2013) in meiotic egg extract supplemented with RanGTP.
evidence: This compares the estimated parameter to values from the literature.

claim: The model recapitulates aster growth with reasonable parameter values and offers a new understanding for how asters grow to span large cytoplasms even when individual microtubules are unstable.
source: Thus, our model recapitulates aster growth with reasonable parameter values and offers a new understanding for how asters grow to span large cytoplasms even when individual microtubules are unstable.
evidence: This is a summary of the model's achievements.

claim: Both plus-end-stimulated and polymer-stimulated nucleation models have qualitatively similar behavior including the gap velocity and recapitulate experimental observations of asters growing as traveling waves.
source: Both models of nucleation have qualitatively similar behavior including the gap velocity and recapitulate experimental observations of asters growing as traveling waves.
evidence: This is a result from comparing different versions of the model.

claim: The qualitative conclusions do not depend on the precise molecular mechanism of autocatalytic nucleation.
source: Thus, in our case, the qualitative conclusions do not depend on the precise molecular mechanism of autocatalytic nucleation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing different models.

claim: The explosive transition characterized by the gap velocity is a general prediction of modeling microtubules as self-amplifying elements whose lifetime depends on their length.
source: In particular, the explosive transition characterized by the gap velocity is a general prediction of modeling microtubules as self-amplifying elements whose lifetime depends on their length.
evidence: This is a general conclusion from the theoretical work.

claim: With polymer-stimulated nucleation, the nucleation rate has units of μm−1 min−1, and describes the number of new microtubules generated per micron of existing microtubule per minute.
source: With polymer-stimulated nucleation, the nucleation rate has units of μm−1 min−1, and describes the number of new microtubules generated per micron of existing microtubule per minute.
evidence: This is a definition of the parameter in the alternative model.

claim: The difference between plus-end-stimulated and polymer-stimulated nucleation has important implications for the structural mechanism of microtubule nucleation and for the prediction of cell-scale phenomena.
source: This difference has important implications for the structural mechanism of microtubule nucleation and for the prediction of cell-scale phenomena.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of distinguishing the mechanisms.

claim: Small mitotic asters are represented by stationary asters found in the regime of bounded polymerization dynamics J<0 and low nucleation rates.
source: Small mitotic asters are represented by stationary asters found in the regime of bounded polymerization dynamics J<0 and low nucleation rates.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the phase diagram in Figure 5.

claim: Model parameters must change as cells transition from mitosis to interphase to produce large growing asters.
source: These model parameters must change as cells transition from mitosis to interphase to produce large growing asters.
evidence: This is an inference from the model about cell cycle regulation.

claim: Polymerization dynamics becomes more favorable to elongation during interphase.
source: Polymerization dynamics becomes more favorable to elongation during interphase (Belmont et al., 1990; Verde et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The change in polymerization dynamics during interphase may be accompanied by an increased autocatalytic nucleation of microtubules.
source: This may be accompanied by an increased autocatalytic nucleation of microtubules.
evidence: This is speculation about cell cycle regulation.

claim: The individual growth regime is inconsistent with the steady-state density of microtubules at the periphery of large asters in both fish and frog embryos.
source: The individual growth regime is also inconsistent with the steady-state density of microtubules at the periphery of large asters in both fish and frog embryos (Ishihara et al., 2014a; Wühr et al., 2008, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental observations.

claim: Experiments in egg extracts confirm the addition of new microtubules during aster growth contrary to the predictions of the standard model.
source: Experiments in egg extracts further confirm the addition of new microtubules during aster growth (Ishihara et al., 2014a) contrary to the predictions of the standard model.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental data.

claim: The collective growth regime is called so because individual microtubules are much shorter (estimated mean length of 16 μm ± 2 μm) than the aster radius (hundreds of microns).
source: We call this the 'collective growth' regime because individual microtubules are much shorter (estimated mean length of 16 μm ± 2 μm, Table 1) than the aster radius (hundreds of microns).
evidence: This is an explanation of the terminology with reference to data.

claim: Predictions of the collective growth model are fully confirmed by the biochemical perturbation via MCAK-Q710.
source: Predictions of this model are fully confirmed by the biochemical perturbation via MCAK-Q710.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental validation.

claim: The finite jump in the aster velocity is in sharp contrast to the prediction of the standard models of spatial growth.
source: The finite jump in the aster velocity (Figure 4) is in sharp contrast to the prediction of the standard models of spatial growth (Fisher, 1937; Kolmogorov and Petrovskii, 1937; Skellam, 1951; van Saarloos, 2003).
evidence: This is a comparison to other models with citations.

claim: Spatial growth is typically modeled by reaction-diffusion processes that account for birth events and random motion, which, in the context of microtubules, correspond to the nucleation and dynamic instability of plus ends.
source: Spatial growth is typically modeled by reaction-diffusion processes that account for birth events and random motion, which, in the context of microtubules, correspond to the nucleation and dynamic instability of plus ends.
evidence: This is a description of standard models.

claim: Reaction-diffusion models neglect internal dynamics of the agents such as the length of a microtubule.
source: Reaction-diffusion models, however, neglect internal dynamics of the agents such as the length of a microtubule.
evidence: This is a critique of standard models.

claim: Reaction-diffusion models inevitably predict a continuous, gradual increase in the aster velocity as the model parameters are varied.
source: As a result, such models inevitably predict a continuous, gradual increase in the aster velocity as the model parameters are varied (Chang and Ferrell, 2013; Hallatschek and Korolev, 2009; Méndez et al., 2007; van Saarloos, 2003).
evidence: This is a statement about the behavior of reaction-diffusion models with citations.

claim: The observation of finite velocity jump provides strong support for the current model and rules out a very wide class of models that reproduce the overall phenomenology of aster growth including the constant velocity and profile shape.
source: The observation of finite velocity jump provides a strong support for our model and rules out a very wide class of models that reproduce the overall phenomenology of aster growth including the constant velocity and profile shape (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a conclusion about model validation.

claim: The theory allows for independent regulation of aster growth rate and microtubule density through the control of the nucleation rate and microtubule polymerization.
source: Our theory allows for independent regulation of aster growth rate and microtubule density through the control of the nucleation rate and microtubule polymerization.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model properties.

claim: Cells have a lot of flexibility in optimizing aster properties and behavior.
source: Thus, cells have a lot of flexibility in optimizing aster properties and behavior.
evidence: This is an inference from the model properties.

claim: The existence of a gap velocity results in switch-like transition from quiescence to rapid growth and allows cells to drastically alter aster morphology with a small change of parameters.
source: The existence of a gap velocity results in switch-like transition from quiescence to rapid growth and allows cells to drastically alter aster morphology with a small change of parameters.
evidence: This is an inference from the model properties.

claim: The rapid growth does not require high microtubule density inside asters, which can be tuned independently.
source: Importantly, the rapid growth does not require high microtubule density inside asters, which can be tuned independently.
evidence: This is an inference from the model properties.

claim: Collective growth produces a meshwork of short microtubules with potentially desirable properties.
source: Collective growth produces a meshwork of short microtubules with potentially desirable properties.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model.

claim: The network is robust to microtubule severing or the spontaneous detachment from the centrosome.
source: First, the network is robust to microtubule severing or the spontaneous detachment from the centrosome.
evidence: This is a predicted property of the collective growth regime.

claim: The network can span arbitrarily large distances yet disassemble rapidly upon mitotic entry.
source: Second, the network can span arbitrarily large distances yet disassemble rapidly upon mitotic entry.
evidence: This is a predicted property of the collective growth regime.

claim: The structure, and therefore the mechanical properties, of the network do not depend on the distance from the centrosome.
source: Third, the structure, and therefore the mechanical properties, of the network do not depend on the distance from the centrosome.
evidence: This is a predicted property of the collective growth regime.

claim: The physical interconnection of the microtubules may facilitate the transduction of mechanical forces across the cell in a way unattainable in the radial array predicted by the standard model.
source: As a speculation, the physical interconnection of the microtubules may facilitate the transduction of mechanical forces across the cell in a way unattainable in the radial array predicted by the standard model (Tanimoto et al., 2016; Wühr et al., 2010).
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance with citations.

claim: The regime of collective growth parallels the assembly of other large cellular structures from short, interacting filaments.
source: The regime of collective growth parallels the assembly of other large cellular structures from short, interacting filaments (Pollard and Borisy, 2003)
evidence: This is a comparison to other biological systems with a citation.

claim: The regime of collective growth is particularly reminiscent of how meiosis-II spindles self-assemble.
source: and is particularly reminiscent of how meiosis-II spindles self-assemble (Burbank et al., 2007; Brugués et al., 2012; Brugués and Needleman, 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison to spindle assembly with citations.

claim: Due to dynamic architecture, spindles are known to have unique physical properties such as self-repair, fusion and scaling.
source: Due to such dynamic architecture, spindles are known to have unique physical properties such as self-repair, fusion (Gatlin et al., 2009) and scaling (Good et al., 2013; Hazel et al., 2013; Wühr et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Dynamic architecture could allow for greater robustness and evolvability.
source: which could allow for greater robustness and evolvability (Kirschner and Gerhart, 1998).
evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation.

claim: Collective growth is one of the most reliable ways for a cell to assemble cytoskeletal structures that exceed the typical length scales of individual filaments.
source: Perhaps, collective growth is one of the most reliable ways for a cell to assemble cytoskeletal structures that exceed the typical length scales of individual filaments.
evidence: This is a concluding speculation about the general significance of the findings.
